name: Multi-catch
desc: Handles several unrelated exception types with one block. The alternatives cannot be subclasses of each other, and the variable only exposes the methods they share.
body:
Order still matters around a multi-catch. A broader clause written above it makes the narrower one unreachable and the compiler rejects the pair. Inside the block, calling a method that exists on only one of the types fails to compile, because the parameter is typed as the closest common supertype.

Do not use `Throwable` or `Exception` in a multi-catch. That is a single wide catch wearing a list, and it hides the failure types the reader needs to see.

name: Checked versus unchecked
desc: A checked failure comes from outside the program and the compiler forces the caller to decide. An unchecked one marks a bug in the caller and needs no throws clause.
body:
The test to apply: can a correct program see this failure and recover? A missing file, a closed socket, a rejected login all pass, so they are checked. A null argument, a negative id, a wrong index all mean the code is wrong, so they are unchecked.

Checked is not a mark of quality. A checked exception that every caller wraps in the same unchecked type adds signatures without adding a decision. On the other hand, wrapping an expected file failure as unchecked forces a catch nobody is told about, so the failure surfaces as a crash.

Subclasses of `RuntimeException` and `Error` are unchecked. Everything else below `Throwable` needs a catch or a `throws` clause, and that includes your own `extends Exception` types.

name: Custom checked exception
desc: A checked type for an expected failure that carries data. Give it a message constructor, a message plus cause constructor, and only the fields a handler really reads.
body:
The class name should say what went wrong, not which layer threw it. `BookingException` tells the handler something; `ServiceException` does not.

Keep the constructors small: `(String message)` and `(String message, Throwable cause)` cover most cases, and a third constructor adds the domain field. A custom exception with no fields and no message building is a rename of `Exception`, so delete it and use a standard type instead.

name: Custom unchecked exception
desc: An unchecked type for a mistake the caller should not repeat. No throws clause anywhere, and one handler at the edge that can still turn it into a message.
body:
Use this when the failure means the caller broke a rule that a check would have caught: a duplicate key, an illegal state transition, a missing required field. The signature stays clean and the compiler stops forcing empty catches.

The trade is discoverability. Nothing in the signature warns the reader, so document it in Javadoc or validate at the entry point. A good compromise is a checked type at the file or network boundary and unchecked types inside the domain.

name: Wrap with the cause
desc: Translates a low level failure into a domain type while keeping the original object as getCause(), so the message and the stack survive.
body:
`getCause()` is the whole point. A wrapped exception without the cause answers what failed but not why. When you catch a low level failure and throw a domain type, pass the caught object as the second argument; when you add context to a runtime failure, `new IllegalStateException("msg", e)` keeps it too.

The message belongs to the operation, not to the driver: which call failed and on which key. The cause carries the vendor text, the SQL state, and the line of code.

Do not wrap the same failure twice on the way up. If a method only adds a layer of signature, it should declare the original type instead of inventing another wrapper.

name: Throwable.addSuppressed()
desc: Attaches a second failure to the one already in flight, so both stay readable and the primary keeps its stack trace.
body:
`addSuppressed` is not only for `close()`. A batch job that must attempt every row can collect failures on one throwable instead of stopping at the first, and the report then shows one failure with its details attached.

A `List<String>` field is the other option, and it is better when the caller has to print a report in its own format. `getSuppressed()` is cheaper to write and keeps the original exception objects, so their messages, causes, and stack traces are still intact.

name: getStackTrace()
desc: Returns the frames captured for one throwable. Frame 0 is the throw site, and the earlier failures live in the cause chain, not in this array.
body:
Each `StackTraceElement` exposes `getClassName`, `getMethodName`, `getFileName`, `getLineNumber`, and `isNativeMethod`. In a log, the first frames name the throw site and the rest show the call path.

The array belongs to the throwable where it was created. When a method wraps a failure, the new exception has its own frames and the original keeps its own, which is why a cause chain prints as several blocks.

Filling the trace costs time. For a control flow exception created in a tight loop, that cost shows up in a profiler; the fix is to stop using an exception there, not to override `fillInStackTrace`.

name: Close order in try-with-resources
syntax: try (A a = open(); B b = open()) { }
desc: Resources close in reverse declaration order, on every exit path, and close failures become suppressed when the body also throws.
body:
The compiler rewrites the header into nested blocks, so the last declared resource closes first. Declare in acquisition order, connection then statement then result set, and the reverse close order is the one those objects need.

If the body throws and `close()` also throws, the body failure stays primary and the close failure lands in `getSuppressed()`. A hand written `finally` cannot do that without explicit bookkeeping, which is the main reason the language form wins.

Java 9 lets an already declared, effectively final variable stand alone in the header: `try (reader) { ... }`. The variable is closed at the end of that block, so do not reuse it afterwards.

name: setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler
desc: Handles failures that no try block caught, on any thread. The last place to log before that thread dies.
body:
The handler runs on the thread that is dying, so keep it short and do not throw from it. It receives the thread and the throwable, which is enough to log the thread name and the full chain.

One handler per thread wins over the default: `thread.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(...)`. The default covers every thread that did not set its own, including the ones a thread pool creates, unless the pool installs its own.

This is a safety net, not a recovery path. A thread that reaches an uncaught handler is gone, and any work it held unfinished stays unfinished.

name: Log once at the boundary
desc: One log record per failure, with the throwable attached. Inner layers wrap and stay silent, so the log shows one incident instead of five.
body:
Passing the throwable as the third argument is what prints the stack. `LOG.severe(e.getMessage())` loses the frames, the cause, and even the type when the message is null.

Decide which layer owns the record. A repository that logs and rethrows, then a service that logs and rethrows, then a controller that logs, writes the same stack three times and makes one failure look like three.

Levels are part of the decision: `WARNING` for a failure that was retried or replaced, `SEVERE` for one the user will notice. In tests, `java.util.logging` can be pointed at a handler that keeps records in memory, which beats reading console output.

name: finally
desc: Runs on every exit path: normal end, caught exception, uncaught exception, return, break, continue. A return inside it discards the pending result.
body:
The block is for cleanup that must happen even when the method leaves early. A `return` in the try block computes its value, then finally runs, then the caller receives the value, so an assignment or a log line in finally still happens first.

Two traps. A `return` inside finally throws away the pending exception and any earlier return value, which is how a real bug becomes a silent wrong answer. `System.exit(0)` skips finally blocks entirely, because the JVM shuts down instead of unwinding the stack.

For anything that implements `AutoCloseable`, use try-with-resources. Keep finally for counters, timers, and legacy close methods, and do not let a second failure in finally replace the one already in flight.

name: Fail fast validation
desc: Rejects a bad argument at the top of the method, with the field name and the received value in the message, before any work is done.
body:
Validate at the point where the value enters, then let the rest of the method work with a value it can trust. A check buried three calls deep costs the reader a stack trace and costs the caller a partial write.

The message should name the field, the accepted range, and the value received. `stars must be 1..5, got 9` answers the question without opening the source.

For user supplied text, validation usually means collecting every problem and throwing one exception that carries the list, not throwing on the first field. `IllegalArgumentException` is for a caller that passed the wrong argument, which is a different situation from a user who typed the wrong value.
